01

Describe & graph data

Explore Quantitative Data

Summary statistics

You need the mean, median, standard deviation, five-number summary, or IQR.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗
Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Exploratory Data Analysis → Explore Quantitative Data

Have ready

A list of quantitative observations.

  1. Choose the Single Variable tab. Under Enter Data, select Your Own.
  2. Select Individual Observations if you have a list of data values.
  3. Enter the variable name and paste your observations into the entry box.
  4. Read the Descriptive Statistics table for the mean, standard deviation, five-number summary, and IQR.
Make sense of the resultIdentify the center and spread, and explain what they mean in the units of your variable.
Explore Quantitative Data

Histograms, boxplots & dotplots

You want to visualize the distribution of a quantitative variable.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗
Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Exploratory Data Analysis → Explore Quantitative Data

Have ready

A list of quantitative observations.

  1. Under Enter Data, select Your Own and choose Individual Observations for a list of data values.
  2. Enter the variable name and paste your observations into the entry box.
  3. Under Choose Type of Plot, check Histogram, Boxplot, or Dotplot as needed. Stem & Leaf is also available.
  4. For a histogram, adjust Select Binwidth for Histogram if your assignment asks for a particular bin width.
Make sense of the resultDescribe shape, center, spread, and any unusual values. Check the axis labels and units.
Explore Categorical Data

Bar graphs & frequency tables

Your observations are categories and you want counts or proportions.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

The example has Pareto Chart checked, which orders bars by frequency. Use the bar-chart settings requested in your assignment.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Exploratory Data Analysis → Explore Categorical Data

Have ready

Category labels or category counts, as requested by the app.

  1. Choose the One Categorical Variable tab.
  2. Under Enter Data, select Individual Observations when entering category labels.
  3. Enter the variable name, then paste category labels into the observations box; the app accepts observations separated by spaces or pasted from a spreadsheet column.
  4. Read the Frequency Table and Bar Graph. Plot Percent changes the graph from counts to percentages.
Make sense of the resultExplain which categories are most common and whether you are comparing counts or proportions.
02

Find probabilities

Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean (Discrete Population)

Expected value

You have a discrete probability distribution and need its long-run mean.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For expected value, use the population mean above the graph. You do not need to click Draw Sample(s); the sample-size and simulation controls serve a different task. Probabilities must be between 0 and 1 and total 1. The original guide notes that calculations may take 30 seconds or more.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem → Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean (Discrete Population)

Have ready

The possible outcomes x and their probabilities P(x).

  1. Under Select Population Distribution, choose Build Custom Distribution.
  2. Enter the Number of distinct values (the number of possible outcomes).
  3. Double-click or double-tap each table cell to enter the outcomes x and probabilities P(x). Check that Total equals 1.
  4. Read the population mean μ above the Population Distribution graph; this is the expected value. The graph also shows the population standard deviation σ.
Make sense of the resultThe expected value is the long-run average over many repetitions; it need not be a possible single outcome.
Binomial Distribution

Binomial probabilities

You count successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗
Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Distributions: Explore Shapes & Find Probabilities → Binomial Distribution

Have ready

Number of trials n, success probability p, and success count x.

  1. Choose Find Probabilities.
  2. Enter the number of trials n and success probability p.
  3. Enter x and choose the inequality that matches the question.
Make sense of the resultTranslate the result into a sentence about the number of successes. Check whether the question says exactly, at least, or at most.
See the guide’s screenshot
Normal Distribution

Normal probabilities

You know a value or interval and want the probability or area for a normal distribution.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For the standard normal distribution, use mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Distributions: Explore Shapes & Find Probabilities → Normal Distribution

Have ready

Mean, standard deviation, and boundary value or values.

  1. Choose Find Probability.
  2. Enter the mean and standard deviation.
  3. Select the probability type (below, above, or between) and enter the boundary value or values.
Make sense of the resultThe shaded area represents the probability. Describe that area using the variable and units from the problem.
See the guide’s screenshot
Normal Distribution

Normal percentiles & quartiles

You know a percentage or probability and want the corresponding value in a normal distribution.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For the standard normal distribution, use mean = 0 and standard deviation = 1. Check whether the input field requests a percent (95) or a decimal (0.95).

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Distributions: Explore Shapes & Find Probabilities → Normal Distribution

Have ready

Mean, standard deviation, and the desired percentile or tail probability.

  1. Choose Find Percentile/Quantile.
  2. Enter the mean and standard deviation.
  3. Choose the percentile type and enter the probability in the format requested by the app.
Make sense of the resultThe output is a cutoff value. State what percentage lies below or above it, using the tail you selected.

03

Estimate with an interval

Inference for a Mean

One-mean t-interval

You estimate a population mean using one sample and an unknown population standard deviation.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

The screenshot demonstrates the settings with a built-in Airbnb dataset. Replace that example with your assignment’s sample. Its displayed 95% interval is $89.91 to $121.97.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Significance Tests (One Sample) → Inference for a Mean

Have ready

Sample data or sample mean, sample standard deviation, sample size, and confidence level.

  1. Choose the Confidence Interval & Significance Test tab.
  2. Select the Enter Data option appropriate to your assignment and enter the sample information. The screenshot uses a built-in textbook example.
  3. Under Type of Inference, select Confidence Interval.
  4. For a usual two-sided interval, select Two-Sided under Bounds; use another choice only if your assignment requests it.
  5. Enter the assigned Confidence Level (%) as a percentage, such as 95 for 95%.
  6. Read the Lower Bound and Upper Bound in the Confidence Interval table.
Make sense of the resultInterpret the interval as an estimate of the population mean, in the units of the variable.
Inference for a Proportion

One-proportion z-interval

You estimate one population proportion from sample successes and a sample size.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For this course: use WALD for the interval method.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Significance Tests (One Sample) → Inference for a Proportion

Have ready

Number of successes, sample size, and confidence level.

  1. Choose Confidence Interval & Significance Test.
  2. Enter the number of successes and sample size.
  3. Choose the confidence level and WALD interval method.
Make sense of the resultInterpret the interval as an estimate of the population proportion in context.
See the guide’s screenshot
Compare Two Proportions

Two-proportion z-interval

You estimate the difference between two population proportions using independent samples.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For this course: use WALD for the interval method.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups → Compare Two Proportions

Have ready

Success counts and sample sizes for both groups, plus a confidence level.

  1. Open Compare Two Proportions.
  2. Use the linked video for the two-proportion interval procedure.
  3. Enter both samples and select WALD for the interval method.
Make sense of the resultInterpret the interval for the difference in proportions. Keep the group order consistent when explaining a positive or negative difference.
04

Test a claim

Inference for a Proportion

One-proportion z-test

You test a claim about one population proportion.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For this course: use SCORE for the test method.

Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Significance Tests (One Sample) → Inference for a Proportion

Have ready

Success count, sample size, null proportion, alternative hypothesis, and significance level.

  1. Open Inference for a Proportion.
  2. Enter the sample information and hypothesized proportion.
  3. Select the alternative hypothesis and SCORE test method; follow the linked example.
Make sense of the resultCompare the p-value with the assigned significance level, then state what the evidence says about the claim.
Compare Two Proportions

Two-proportion z-test

You test whether two population proportions differ using independent samples.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗

For this course: use SCORE for the test method.

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups → Compare Two Proportions

Have ready

Success counts and sample sizes for both groups, alternative hypothesis, and significance level.

Compare Two Means

Independent two-sample t-test

You compare population means for two independent groups.

Open Art of Stat ↗Watch the example ↗
Show steps & reminders

Find the app

Confidence Intervals & Tests Comparing Two Groups → Compare Two Means

Have ready

Two independent samples or their summary statistics, plus the assigned test settings.

Two matched columns of quantitative measurements.

Inference for Comparing Several Groups → Chi-Squared Test
